KEY MESSAGE 1...A few showers possible across the interior near 
daybreak Thu. Otherwise...a widespread cold rain focused later Thu 
into Fri. Rain may flip to or mix with wet snow with the greatest 
risk for that in the high terrain. Any snow accumulations look minor 
at this time.

Low pressure across the north central plains will shift eastward 
tonight and emerge off the mid-Atlantic coast Thu. This low will 
intensifies as it tracks near or inside the Benchmark into Friday. 
We will break things down in much greater detail below. 

As the surface low moves east tonight...mid/high level cloudiness 
will begin to overspread the region. As the system approaches the 
mid-Atlantic a S-SE low level jet will develop near daybreak across 
the interior. This may result in some lower clouds along with a few 
showers developing at this time as well. As this low pressure system 
emerges off the coast...a modest E low level jet will develop during 
the day Thursday. However...model soundings indicate that there is a 
lot of dry low level air hanging around along the coastal plain...so 
much of Thu may end up dry/cloudy with just a few spot showers. 
Therefore...bulk of showers on Thu likely confined to the interior 
for much of the day and amounts on the lighter side. 

The steady/widespread rain will overspread the region Thu after 4-5 
pm into the evening hours as deeper forcing/moisture arrives. This 
will be a result of the surface low pressure intensifying as it 
passes near or just inside the Benchmark into Fri. 
Therefore...expect a cold rain for much of the region Thu night into 
Fri. The question then becomes do thermal profiles become cold 
enough for the rain to flip to a period of wet snow. Thermal 
profiles are very marginal and the exact track of the mid level 
centers along with precipitation intensity will determine if this 
happens. Right now the greatest potential for this is across the 
interior high terrain...mainly the east slopes of the 
Berks/Worcester Hills. However...some of the guidance especially the 
REFS indicate a track further south. This actually brings the 
greater risk of wet snow further south into the CT/RI Hills. In 
fact...there is even a low risk for rain to briefly mix/change with 
wet snow even right the I-95 corridor. We should have a better idea 
on this potential in the next 24 hours...but regardless any impacts 
will likely be rather limited at this point. A coating to 2" of 
slushy wet snow is a possibility in the high terrain with a low risk 
of 3". Greatest risk for this would be at elevations near or above 
800 feet and particularly near 1500 feet. Of course this will be 
dependent on the track of the 700 mb low pressure system and if 
precipitation rates can be heavy enough.  

The other story on Friday will be the unseasonably cold 
temperatures. Given N low level flow along with clouds and 
precipitation...daytime temperatures will generally be in the 30s to 
the lower 40s! Bulk of the precipitation should wind down later 
Fri...but a few left over showers can not be ruled out near the 
coast Fri night.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Cool with mainly dry conditions Saturday through 
early next week. 

The surface low pressure system slowly shifts further eastward into 
the Atlantic Saturday. The bulk of the precipitation will have 
exited with the low. While it will likely be dry in most areas, 
residual moisture flow may support some isolated/"pop-up" showers. A 
below normal airmass will be positioned across the region supporting 
highs in the mid to upper 40s with the higher terrain areas in the 
upper 30s to low 40s. Breezy NW winds make temperatures feel more 
like the mid 30s to low 40s. Expect a chilly night Saturday night 
with temperatures falling into the 20s and 30s. High pressure slowly 
builds in from the west Sunday into early next week bringing a 
period of dry conditions. Another breezy cool day Sunday with winds 
decreasing by Monday as the pressure gradient relaxes. Temperatures 
slowly moderate closer to seasonable values Tue/Wed.
